$comment: The live Roblox activity page and the stock page. Every sentence here draws a line between what Roblox published, what this site observed, and what nobody knows — so none of them may be shortened into a claim the data does not support.

platformFigure.floorHeading: This is a floor, not a platform total.
platformFigure.floorBody: Roblox publishes no live figure for the whole platform and this site does not estimate one. Roblox ranks a small share of the experiences it hosts, so the real number of people playing is higher than this — by how much, nobody outside Roblox can say.

method.heading: How this page gets its numbers
method.liveBody: Fetched server-side from Roblox when the page is served and cached for {minutes} minutes. Your browser makes no request to Roblox, and no script from Roblox runs on this page.
method.historyBody: A scheduled job records one observation every {interval} minutes. Platform totals keep every one of them for {retention} days; per-experience counts keep one an hour for {gameDays} days, because that is one array per experience across several hundred of them. Both charts show what was actually recorded, gaps included — nothing is averaged to fill the runs not kept.
method.provenanceTitle: Ranking and counts are Roblox’s, the record is ours
method.provenanceBody: Which experiences appear, how many players each has, and how each has been voted on all come from Roblox. This site does not rank experiences, does not estimate player counts, and does not publish a figure it did not either read from Roblox or observe itself and label as such. The approval share is the only arithmetic on this page, and it is Roblox’s own up and down vote counts divided. For the money side of the platform, see {payoutStatisticsLink}, which come from Roblox’s filings.

download.heading: Download these observations
download.description: Exactly what was collected, with the gaps left in.
download.innerDescription: The observations behind the chart above, as a spreadsheet or as JSON. Read from storage; downloading makes no request to Roblox.

limitations.noInterpolation: Observations only. Nothing is interpolated and no missing observation is filled in — a gap means the collector did not run, and it is left visible rather than smoothed over.
limitations.cadence: Collected every 15 minutes. Platform totals are kept 14 days; per-experience series are sampled hourly and kept 7 days, so the two files have different resolutions and different spans.
limitations.coverage: Covers only the experiences Roblox was ranking at the moment of each observation. This is not all of Roblox, and no share of the platform can be worked out from it.
limitations.rowProvenance: Every row carries its own observation time and origin, so a row copied elsewhere still says what it is.

stock.intro: Roblox’s reported results, and an honest account of why there is no live share price here yet.
stock.reportedResultsCaption: Roblox’s reported results for the most recent quarter, against the same quarter a year earlier.
stock.quotedFrom: Quoted from {source}, not recomputed here. A fuller breakdown, including what Roblox pays creators each quarter, is on {payoutStatisticsLink}.
stock.noChartHeading: Why there is no embedded chart
stock.noChartBody: Sites that show a live Roblox chart are almost always embedding one from a market data vendor, which means that vendor’s script runs in your browser and can see your visit. This site loads no third-party scripts on any page, and adding one here would quietly undo that for everyone.
stock.whenConnected: When a provider is connected it will be read server-side and rendered as plain HTML, so the price arrives the same way every other figure on this site does: fetched by the server, attributed, and dated.
stock.notAdviceBody: Nothing on this page is a recommendation to buy or sell anything. A company’s results say nothing about what any individual creator will be paid, and the DevEx rate is set by Roblox independently of its share price.
stock.notLatestBody: This is the most recent quote this site received. {reason} The price above is unchanged from when it was taken; nothing has been adjusted to look current.

stats.intro: What Roblox actually pays creators, taken from its own filings with the SEC. Every figure below links to the document it came from.
stats.payoutsDescription: Developer exchange fees are a line on Roblox’s income statement: the money it paid out through DevEx. It is the closest thing to a measure of what the creator economy earns.
stats.byYearChartCaption: Developer exchange fees by financial year, as reported by Roblox.
stats.byYearTableCaption: Roblox developer exchange fees by financial year, with the filing each figure comes from.
stats.byQuarterDescription: Roblox reports quarterly, so this is the finest resolution that exists. Two quarters are marked as derived: they are a six-month total minus the quarter Roblox printed, which is exact arithmetic but not a figure Roblox published on its own.
stats.byQuarterChartCaption: Developer exchange fees by quarter. Hollow bars are derived by subtraction rather than reported directly.
stats.byQuarterTableCaption: Roblox developer exchange fees by quarter, showing which figures were reported and which were derived.
stats.rateTimelineHeading: What one Robux has been worth
stats.rateTableLabel: DevEx rates and what they pay
stats.rateTableCaption: Each documented DevEx rate and the payout it produces for 100,000 eligible Earned Robux.
stats.usageHeading: How many people use Roblox, and for how long
stats.twoFiguresTitle: Two figures other trackers show, and this page does not
stats.noSharePriceTitle: There is no share price on this page, on purpose
stats.downloadDescription: The rows behind the charts, with every figure labelled reported or derived.
stats.downloadInnerDescription: Everything charted on this page, plus the metrics Roblox does not publish, as a spreadsheet or as JSON.

limitations.reportedOrDerived: Every row states whether Roblox reported the figure or this site derived it from reported ones. The derivations are described on the methodology page.
limitations.exactDecimal: Money is carried as an exact decimal string, never as a floating-point number, and never rounded on the way out.
limitations.filingLinked: Each row names the filing it came from and links to it, so any figure can be checked against the original document.
limitations.absencesIncluded: The metrics Roblox does not publish are included as absences with reasons, not omitted — a file without them would look like the complete picture.

business.p2: A live RBLX quote would need a paid market-data feed and a third-party script running in your browser. This site loads no third-party scripts, and a number it cannot trace to a document is a number it will not publish. The figures above come from the filing itself, which is the same source a share price ultimately reacts to. None of this is investment advice, and a quarterly result says nothing about what any individual will be paid.

whatItMeans.p1: Very little, directly — and that is worth saying plainly. The totals on this page describe the whole platform. They do not change what your own balance converts to, they are not a forecast, and a rising total does not mean a rising rate. What decides your payout is the rate applied to your eligible Earned Robux, which you can work out on
whatItMeans.p2: The one thing these figures do show is scale: DevEx is a programme through which Roblox paid out
whatItMeans.p3: in a single year, which is context worth having before deciding whether the 30,000 Robux minimum is worth working towards.

noLiveData.p1: Roblox publishes these numbers once a quarter, in a filing. That is the finest resolution that exists, so a chart claiming to show them changing by the minute would be showing something invented. This site runs no data collection, samples nothing and estimates nothing — it reads the filings and links to them.

prose.quarterOfRevenue: The line worth reading twice is the second one. Developer exchange fees are about a quarter of Roblox’s revenue, so a meaningful share of what the platform takes in leaves again as creator payouts. Every figure in this table is quoted from {filings}.
prose.precision: Figures are recorded to the precision the filing used. Where Roblox reported in thousands the amount is exact to the dollar; where it reported in millions, it is exact to the million and no further. Two quarters are marked as derived because they come from subtracting a reported quarter from a reported six-month total. Read more about how this site handles figures in {methodology}.
prose.whatItMeansIntro: Very little, directly — and that is worth saying plainly. The totals on this page describe the whole platform. They do not change what your own balance converts to, they are not a forecast, and a rising total does not mean a rising rate. What decides your payout is the rate applied to your eligible Earned Robux, which you can work out on {calculator}.
